header.title: Libellus Adversus eos qui contra Synodum Scribere Praesumpserunt: AI translation (Claude)
header.author: Ennodius, Magnus Felix
header.source: Translated by Claude (claude-opus-5-5, Anthropic) from the library's stoa0114a.stoa012.opp-lat1, from Open Greek and Latin's CSEL (CC BY-SA 4.0), one English line for each line of the original. The whole work is translated. It was chosen because no English translation of it could be found.
header.statement: An AI-generated translation of the whole work, checked against the original by a second AI only in samples. No specialist has reviewed it.

notes.urn:cts:latinLit:stoa0114a.stoa012.opp-l: Ref 1: 'nisi cum necessariam dicendi nimis ineptam esse condicionem' is defective as printed (probably a garbled Ciceronian allusion); translated for the evident sense. 'nonis nexibus' read as 'nouis'. Ref 4: 'aetate ualentes' (strong in age) contradicts the argument; translated as 'advanced in age', assuming a corruption (e.g. 'graues' or 'labentes'). 'Cepasius' is an orator named by Cicero (Brutus), apparently cited ironically. Ref 5: 'Militibus' is printed with a capital; sense uncertain, perhaps ironic. 'caloe' read as 'calce'. 'quis' in 'Psalm' citation 'furem uidebas' is Ps. 49(50):18. Ref 6: 'prohibetis' (you forbid) fits the opponents' argument poorly; the original may have read 'non prohibetis' (you do not forbid). 'potest optare quia alteri quod ipse iam perdidit' is awkward and may be corrupt.

Line 7: the final 'P' is read as a question mark. Line 8: 'lacob' is read as Iacob. In Genesis it is Isaac, not Jacob, who blesses, and the text's 'Jacob' (twice) may be Ennodius' own slip or a corruption. 'gruentem' is probably corrupt (perhaps for 'non congruentem' or 'incongruentem'); it is translated as 'at odds with'. Line 9: 'ineluctatae' is obscure and is translated as 'unresisted'. The sentence beginning 'Does anyone decree the outcome...' ('dum inquisitione esse senior innotescit') is difficult, and the rendering is tentative. The closing 'P' is read as '?'. Line 10: 'ad defraudationem genii pertinere' is obscure; it is rendered literally. A lacuna follows 'exuli exilium imperas nec das', and the quotation breaks off. 'quam sponte prolata m illis non habere non poterat' seems corrupt (perhaps 'prolatam in illis'); the subject '[their condition]' is supplied. 'ia' is read as 'in' and 'ui.ri' as 'uiri'. Line 11: 'P' is read as '?'.

Line 13: 'festinantem animam morti non credidit uni' appears to be a verse quotation (cf. Lucan); the sentence 'potesne ... feriari' is printed without a question mark and is taken as a question. Line 15: in the Isaiah quotation the text reads 'nobis' ('to us') where the biblical text has 'vobis' ('to you'); translated as given. Line 16: 'criminosi etsi est meritum, tollit accusator' is obscure; the sense seems to be that the accuser, by his fury, forfeits the just punishment the guilty man deserved. Line 17: the stray full stop before 'describat' is ignored; the clause 'quae grauis est plerumque principibus inpugnatio, minus fidelium blanditiis non legatur' is uncertain in construction and the rendering is tentative. Scanning errors read as: 'ilia' = illa (15), 'ia' = in (18).

Scanning errors read as: 'Fost' = Post, 'squis' = sedis, 'diseidii' = dissidii, 'ab ipse' = ab ipso, 'de fensio' = defensio, 'Eseiae' = Esaiae; duplicated 'et et' treated as one. Line 21: 'laesum principem, quare...' construed as 'the prince was injured because'; 'ut nihil amplius liceret...' taken as giving the synod's motive. Line 22: 'apostoli genio decerpi' is obscure; rendered 'the apostle's spirit is diminished'. Line 23: 'nisi princeps fastidii summa moderetur' is obscure and possibly corrupt; translated literally. Line 24: 'canum' taken as 'canum' = ancient; 'qui per culpas iuuenescit' is difficult.

26: 'nec dum essetis agrestes' is obscure; rendered as 'has not yet carried you off into wildness'. 'concordise' read as 'discordiae'. 26: 'hunc elegi ... utrosque reppuli' follows the text as given; the sense of 'this one' (Boniface or Symmachus) is unclear. 27: 'ei inter deum' read as 'et'; 'ei uerbis eius' read as 'in uerbis eius'; 'linguae oratione sed gemituum' appears corrupt, translated by sense. 28: 'nitri' read as 'uiri' (Ps. 75:6, 'dormierunt somnum suum viri divitiarum'); 'auris congruam sortita grauitatem' is uncertain. 29: 'impietatem' may be an error for 'pietatem' ('compassion'). 25: 'cumbulam' read as 'cymbulam' (skiff).

30: 'quasi obsoleta corporatos communione' is obscure; rendered 'incorporated in an outworn communion'. 'affectu(s aut cu)i' follows the edition's restoration. 'anaritia' read as 'avaritia'; 'qui\'' read as 'quae'. 32: 'ei orbatae' read as 'si orbatae'; 'd adisse' read as 'doluisse'; 'ia tali' as 'in tali'. 33: 'ad M uenientes' read as 'ad se uenientes'; 'feuistis' read as 'fouistis'. The opening of 33 ('pretiosis siccamus ubera partubus') is difficult; translated literally.

nodes.text: II. A Pamphlet against Those Who Presumed to Write against the Synod.
PREFACE.

The fervour of many motives commonly calls forth the urge to speak: either the mind is greedy for praise and wishes to buy favour with its sweat, so that, through the blandishments of glory, it disregards the torment of the one who speaks; or, bound in the fetters of gain, it sells the service of its tongue, so that while the mind, subdued by the desire to possess, reckons that it already holds the profit it has counted on, it does not know enough to fear the dangers that bear down through the use of the pen; or, hemmed in by necessity, it brings out a captive eloquence without any polish of the file and displays in public a brow that knows no shame, so that, while it serves its purpose, it forswears care for elegance. For the ornaments of speech belong not to business but to repose, and painted words belong not to warfare but to leisure. The battlefield demands a strong man, deep peace a garlanded one: he who asserts what will do good despises speech coloured by the brush of art. This being so, I introduce the cause of my account and commend to devout minds a voice forced out by the barking of the wicked, remembering that it is written: a time to keep silent, a time to speak; or, after the assurance of the prophetic oracle, the example of a certain orator, who says that the condition of speaking is quite unfitting except when it is necessary. I therefore devote the service of my mouth, as far as the strength of my talent allows, to the bishops, against whom the venom of hissing tongues has been poured out, although devout patience, defended by the shield of faith, does not fear the shower of darts, and weapons aimed without skill in fighting return upon their author. For those who have Christ as their breastplate do not fear violence, and lay their enemies low by long waiting. Yet would anyone think a battle in this line a cause for fear, in which war is waged against God and the pontiffs without any reckoning of strength? Would anyone, seeing a slack enemy who only provokes, dread an adversary weak in the causes for which he fights? He begrudges himself the victory who holds back from attacking an enemy wounded by his own conscience. He advances to his enemy's profit who, in conflicts, weighs anything else before the causes. Innocence gives strength to javelins, and the will to fight, when it comes from justice, sharpens the blade: we know that just grievance, more than arms, has given the force to strike. Hence a multitude has not withstood the weapons of a few. So, with the prophet saying with me: more are with us than with them, I shall begin a work that, as I reckon, will please the good.

It would indeed suffice that schismatic ignorance has fallen by its very proposition, especially since the objections carry their own answer with them, and the title deserves to be condemned together with its author without any examination of the reading, since in the heading itself the meaning of the unclean work is made known, saying: AGAINST THE SYNOD OF UNFITTING ABSOLUTION. Nevertheless I shall now proceed as if the one who proposes evil needed to perish by another's sword. This preface, you most demented of men, can be ascribed only to ignorance. Is there anyone but you to be counted among the ulcerous and straying sheep, who could have assailed the great flock of shepherds, when the prophet says: I have nourished and raised up sons, but they have despised me; and the Lord says of the apostles: whoever despises you despises me — and the prophet testifies that they were bishops, saying of Judas: and let another take his bishopric — and the apostle Paul likewise proclaims: obey those set over you, for they will pray for you?

But let us return to that weighty and venerable proposition, not merely brought out of a pigsty but mephitic. 'Not all the bishops,' they say, 'did the king's authority summon to the council, nor did all agree in the judgment.' Slaves of Tartarus and plainly ministers of Satan, whoever was not called by the prince's letter was drawn in by your cause, with new bonds and with the coils of your doings. I do not wish to say with what wish, with what intention they departed, those in whom that waiting bred weariness, when they saw that the venerable pope had received a long respite in life, contrary to what they held right. They saw that only the air was struck by the darts they had aimed. So that these unhappy men might not be allowed to lurk in secret, consoling themselves in their evil deeds, the hidden are laid bare by your books, and through you they are not permitted to keep their solitude in a shameful act, as the Lord says in the Gospels: everyone who is evil hates the light.

After this you assert that those who accused the aforesaid by presenting petitions ought not to have been called adversaries of the Roman pope, adding, to confirm the assertion, that the royal orders had not called them by this name. O men shaped by every file of art and smelted in smiths' furnaces, who have found hard-sweated testimonies to back up what you say! We love your opinion, reverend sirs, and, as they say, we go over to it on foot: we acknowledge the errors you speak of. Would anyone call an accuser an enemy, and give a tragic name to one who does not deserve insult? Next you clasped on the attached question with a rhetorical brooch, alleging: 'The Roman city is witness whether all the bishops who assembled were old and feeble.' Behold a speech gleaming with the sinews of truth, to be preferred to Cepasius himself for the polish of its language! So, because they said they were advanced in age and feeble in body, they themselves testify that they are unfit for judgment, since they said they already suffered the decay of their limbs — especially if they presumed to press this upon the ears of our most clement lord. Do you suppose — you who have been driven from all the sight of God — that, after the fashion of your own gatherings, everything to be reported is everywhere thrown into confusion, and that before the prince others spoke about the assembly of pontiffs than those whom the ripeness of their age made the leaders in opening the address, on whom their many years had conferred reverence, who were thought to have been preserved so long by the support of good merits? It was fitting, then, that those should complain of the weariness of heavy age whom age had appointed to plead. Most excellent men, you added that from the royal orders the cause of the summons was already known, and that the ruler of all Italy need not have been consulted as if about a new matter: more was owed to the document and to the writing of religion than to the prince's presence. So no head of charge remained in the aforesaid matter, proceeding to the inquiry into which they might rightly have given that opening speech. Then, digressing, you praise in the king his disposition towards good things, and you cultivate in words the innocence you do not know in deeds — if indeed there is any cultivation in your speech, which you break up with a rough ploughshare, as if driving your ploughs off the track, entrusting darnel to withered soil, to receive for such outlay chaff by which the fire of Gehenna may be kindled to your ruin.

But now, as someone is reported to have said, what shall I put before what? Contrary to the apostle, you say that the assailants of the supreme pontiff were not heard, men who, mindful of the heavenly command, withdrew their share from fellowship with an adulterer. Here I do not attack your ignorance, I do not accuse your leaky memory. I do not wish to say that you attributed the prophet's words to the apostle, since I know that those too are rightly called apostles who, as I am well aware, were sent. For David says: you saw a thief and ran with him, and with adulterers you placed your portion. Next, who could untangle himself from that question of yours in which you say: 'Among the crimes alleged, what is not excluded is proved'? Behold a saying befitting the soldiers of the Roman church, in which you would not know whether to praise first its polish or its flavour! Have you, I ask, heard it read: what is just you shall pursue justly? Have you heard, concerning men's misdeeds — if indeed human society ever held you — that whatever is not proved by its proper procedures is excluded? Where is that saying of the prophet: the Lord will come to judgment with the elders of his people; and the one said of you: they proclaimed their sin like Sodom: woe to their souls? But what is to be done, whenever no remedy comes to the aid of the desperate, except to implore the Lord, who promised through the prophet that he would come upon everyone proud and lofty and upon everyone arrogant, that he may be brought low? But I shall follow the stinking work in its tracks and, if I can, crush it with an iron-shod heel, so that, to speak truly, fact will fight with fact, case with case, reason with what they suppose to be reason. You allege that the bishops spoke against the royal orders, and you believe it a kind of sacrilege, something wicked — though you do not know the command of the heavenly Lord — to think differently from the command of the earthly lord, objecting: who ought to have told the king that the pope should have convoked the synod? Surely, what precedent stands in this matter? Him above all, who already lay prostrate under the criminal charges of many; for whom to be accused would have been to be condemned; whose prerogative, ascribed to him from heaven, the denunciation of his enemies would already have taken away? To this madness the growth of evil deeds has drawn you step by step, that you believe accusing to be the same as convicting, and that with you hatreds differ in nothing from truth — hatreds which, for the most part, against the merit of the accused, put together wishes that obey partisanship, not reason? Where is that saying: before you know, do not judge anyone? Long ago the flock placed on the left received you as colleagues, among whom he who deserved to be brought to examination is believed to have received his sentence by prejudgment, and to enter the scales of dispute is to become guilty.

To your preface, however, you most excellently added a divine example, which is made up of such well-squared phrases that you would think Chrysippus himself was keeping the line in it: to the sinner God says: why do you recount my righteous acts? Joining to this saying a kind of apostrophe, as it were, to the bishops: 'Because he is reckoned the vicar of the blessed apostle Peter, you forbid the chief physician to bring medicine to his body: how [then] do you refuse to provide care for his soul?' Whether this is a great joke in divine matters or the greatest cause for lament, I do not know. You seek a cure for another's fever, you desire a remedy to be applied to a failing soul, and, placed close to death and forgetful of yourselves, you deliberate about another's health. What if that was truly said to you by the prophet: is it a small thing that you are troublesome to men? you are troublesome also to my God; and again: physician, heal yourself? But more of this elsewhere. We know that one who has been given up cannot be healed, and the shameless man, sinking into the depth, despises [all] with amazing rashness. But I believe that even in these men, even in the death of their evil way of life, there is still some judgment alive, and one may wish for another what he himself has already lost. Now I shall rightly say with the prophet: all that this people speaks is conspiracy, and do not fear its fear nor dread it. Let this itching of tongues that is among us be gone from us — those whom the same prophet truly rebukes: writing, you have written injustice. We do not judge, as you claim, that the blessed Peter or his successors received from the Lord, together with the privileges of the see, a licence to sin. He sent down to posterity a perpetual dowry of merits together with the inheritance of innocence: what was granted to him for the light of his deeds belongs to those whom a like splendour of life illuminates. For who would doubt that he is holy whom the summit of so great a dignity raises up? In him, if goods acquired by merit are lacking, those supplied by his predecessor in that place suffice. For either it raises the illustrious to these heights, or it makes illustrious those who are raised: for he foreknows what is fit for the foundation of the churches, upon whom the whole structure itself rests. But hence you think that the heavenly power is supported by your deeds, because you lend, as you say, a helping right hand for the protection of the blessed apostle. Do you not know, you fools, that the sun is not aided by torches, nor are lamps lit to protect the light of day? For it is written: God searches the hearts and the reins.

But on that point who would dare to answer your arguments, except that truth is spoken without art, while credence is stitched onto falsehood by the tricks of words? "Why," they say, "did you come to the prince, if it was not permitted for the accused to be heard?" Does the fog of sin, or a divine dread, so smear you over into the stupor of cattle that your mind either passes over a modest excuse through deceit or, weighed down by the dullness of beasts, does not recognise it? Or perhaps you think that what was said meant something else, namely that he himself, whose office was needed, ought to have convoked the synod, so that the divine sentence might strike you down through a pontifical examination, you whom an insane fervour had cut off from the joining of your head, to the loss of your salvation?

After this you put into your work, with words or with barks I do not know, a mention of Esau, comparing to him your own bishop, as one who lost the benefit of elder birth in exchange for a single dish and forfeited the venerable dignity of the firstborn by obeying his gullet. What shall I reply to this, hemmed in as I am on every side of your objections? Which of you, I ask, snatched the blessing from Symmachus while he served his father the more? On whom was the nobility of such great gifts conferred by the voice of Jacob? Which of you, ready to obey the wishes of a blind parent, came to meet him? Which of you, by his devotion, made a venerable father deprived of his eyes feel no loss of light? Is not night, compared with your darkness, thought to show a radiance shining through a clear sky, and does not all obscurity, compared with your deeds, take on the beauty of the sun? Moreover, Jacob then, though [it was] at odds with his son's character, nevertheless conferred the blessing already promised. Now why do we linger longer over these things, since those who have kicked against the goads cannot be taught? Believe me, what you put forward is hostile to peace, and not fit for an attack.

But there follows a knot together with a riddle, which I do not know by what art of reply we may untie. For having entered the sea of Ciceronian depth, they drive our little boat with blasts of questions through the uncertainties of the shores. In it, however, with Christ holding the helm, I shall enter port and examine one by one all your whirlwinds, having in steering through them a capacity not my own. For they say: "If the assertion of the bishops is true, that the prelate of the apostolic see has never been subject to the judgment of lesser men, why was he brought to judgment by a strict summons?" Much indeed does an aged infancy labour in me here, for which He must be called on who always overcomes with us the weight of an unresisted proposition, since I openly cry out for the bishops with the prophet: Shall the axe boast against him who cuts with it? Or shall the saw exalt itself against him who draws it? So that this divine oracle may support me: As when the exactor has ceased, the tribute rests, so the Lord has broken the staff of the wicked. Grant, Lord, what you foretold of them, that as the drunkard staggers and vomits, so may the unbeliever perish who acts faithlessly. For this reason the prophet cries out, mocking you: Hear the word of the Lord, you scornful men. Does anyone decree the outcome of cases from foreknowledge, and, when about to set an end to raging conflicts, so measure it that a hasty decision, when it becomes known to be older than the inquiry, betrays the partiality of the judge? Now for a little while, unworthy as I am in speech, in deeds and in years, I shall rebuke you with a bishop's voice. We, who did not wish our statutes to be weighed by you on a single scale; for whom canons have been passed concerning the character of accusers; among whom it is wrong to overstep the venerable decisions of the fathers; for whom it is written in the council of Carthage, which the authority of the apostolic see approved through bishop Faustinus, who was then present, sent by it, that accusers coming out of an enemy's house are not to be believed, in whom a neighbourhood inflamed by hatred stirs up the flame of persecution with dry fuel and, by secret arrangement, assembles the whole fabric of deceit with money and contrivances fitted together: how could our assembly have known what house had spewed these men out, unless they were present, and from where could it have learned the character of the attack, except from a written charge? In which it would have recognised the bilge of crimes, while they pretend that they owe a prosecution to crimes?

After what was said about the accusers, you added, as to why the persons whom imperial authority had often demanded were ordered to be produced, that this amounted to defrauding the genius of him who now stands in the apostolic see as in a kind of citadel. Truly Wisdom says to you: A man who is weak and of short life will not attain understanding, but let him labour to know what is acceptable to the Lord; and again Proverbs say: He who neglects study hates himself, for death meets the unskilled. Why do you feign that ignorance which comes down from viperine knowledge? Why do you employ illusions with a wondrous art of robbery, showing simplicity on your brow? Truly it has been said of you: He who speaks a lie speaks from his own. That face of gladness that comes from the verdict of a court you removed from the eyes of your bishop by crafty foresight, so that, when he was equipped with such defences against your battle lines and was carrying the weapons of innocence in the testimony of the world, you might drive him from the very sanctuaries of the court, taking care that the innocent man should neither live free of attack nor, when assailed, have the comfort of an uncorrupted inquiry by judges. You both granted and begrudged the aforesaid a hearing, since on one and the same road he is both forbidden and forced by you to undergo the hazards of disputation, and is summoned along a single path to the case only to be kept away from it, so that he might neither obtain manifest safety unchallenged nor snatch it by acquittal. I remember having read in the days of my youth what was said of someone: "You order exile for an exile and do not give [...]" The prophet's sentence assails you: These are the men who troubled the earth and who shook kingdoms; and again: Their little branches shall be cut off with pruning hooks, and what is left shall be cut away; and again: When you do not expect it, your crushing shall come, and your multitude shall be broken like a potter's jar; and also the prophet, speaking specially to this case, thundered: The Lord will stretch out his hand, and he who brings help to the wicked shall fall, and he to whom help is given shall fall, and all together shall be consumed. Yet after the old refuges of examples I return to the newer definitions of the canons. The council of Carthage cries out in another place: Whatever persons the public laws do not admit to accusation, from them we too remove the licence to attack another. I ask you, men in whom a perfection polished to the fingernail is set, of what condition were those slaves whom you requested by the prince's letters? If a servile chain still held them in another's power, and no steps sent out into freedom loosed them from the fetters of a base bondage, would the words of the aforesaid have carried any credibility even with you as disputants? But, I suppose, you will reply: the truth which [their condition] could not but lack in them when freely offered, the religious torturer had extracted from its hiding places by various torments, so that, while their bodies were broken by pains, the soul would not conceal what it knew had been done. But I ask you, turn your faces first to the public laws, then to the judges, who can speak thus in their own defence: "Shall we, whom the service of God has made freeborn after casting off these things, who either despise or laugh at the insults of jeering slaves, to whom it is written by the apostle concerning servants: Remember that your Lord and theirs is in heaven, be called back to these evils of the world? Must we do what we maintain makes another who does it profane? Shall what would defile our sight through the ministry of a command and another's hand be carried out at our order?" Do not keep this mind towards all the churches in the manner and nature of rapacious wolves, because even after a bloody examination had perhaps stained us according to your desires, it would not have had among them the effect you aim at. But, as the prophet tells us, let us put a ring in your nostrils and a bridle on your lips, and lead you back on the way by which you came, you who are assailed, as the same prophet asserts, who says: They shall be as if they were not, and the men who contradict you shall perish.

This too you added against us as a new invention: that our very Lord and Redeemer submitted to the judgments of servants, and the maker of heaven willingly subjected himself to a certain earthly particle, when he testifies and says: Man of Judah, and you who dwell in Jerusalem, judge between me and my vineyard. You relate that blessed Peter and the apostle Paul did not shrink from this either, and you drag that elegance of yours into a point of law, advancing with chains of examples, as if a contest with an opponent remained for you on this point and what is freely offered had to be wrung out by the strong fingers of your eloquence. You say that the wonderful prophet Samuel too implored the testimony of the people to the serenity of his conscience. For what did Samuel say? That the Lord knew he had never taken anyone's property nor driven off anyone's cattle, that he had resisted bribes and, what is beyond human nature, had avoided gifts that came of their own accord, taking care, namely, not to suffer harm to his reputation through the prejudgments of suspicion. Lastly he revealed his innocence under divine attestation, so as not to undergo human examination. Our Redeemer, when he looks at your wickedness in the present business, rather invokes the judgment which he wishes to take place between himself and his vineyard. Saint Athanasius, bishop of the city of Alexandria, when he was accused through the envy of your partners, recognising that the multitude of insults brought him exercise, not fear, truly added to the price of his crown what he lowered of his dignity, and before the heavenly sentence of acquittal, being a good judge of innocence, he played the part of the accused. For thus the soldiers of Christ bring forth by their sweat increases of honour for themselves, while they chasten the heights granted them with a loftier humility, and will purchase heaps of praise from the very fact that they govern the summits they have attained with sublime restraint. But although his see shows blessed Athanasius to be, so far as one may know, unequal to the Roman bishop, yet in conduct they are comparable in their affairs. He presented himself to the judges; this one, as even you say, summoned them. He, as a servant of God, did not flee the inquiry threatened against him; this one placed the hope of his triumph in the assembly of the examiners. But why should we linger longer over these comparisons? This one too wanted, loved, drew on and entered judgment, and, what could rouse the hearts of the faithful with the stings of just grief, granted the venerable council authority even against himself, if he deserved it. Who, at this outset of his pleading, would not know that he came to his fellow bishops supported by testimonies of purity, he who shrank from what was less permitted to their strictness, judging that what an invalid judge had decreed should rather be undone in any way possible? Why do you attack the aforesaid with dog-like loquacity? Why do you harm one who does not deserve it? His wish is what you think is your threat; but the venom of a new serpent hisses more cunningly in you than in the adversaries of Athanasius. They did not know what you know very well: how triumph might be taken from the accused. They feared that the man summoned might not appear to be heard; you, not bearing the delay that the examinations involved, drove him back with javelins as he came, and exchanged the weariness of awaiting the sentence prepared for you for the taking up of avenging arms. O recollection of evils, which both supplies the voice and undermines it, while the very gravity of the deed confounds the words of those whom it has driven to cry out!

Who could bear your chatter with patience? So, by your assertion, we do not love the advantages of a new usefulness, because we show obedience to what our elders have defined? Here you hoist every sail of your wit; here the belch of your upturned neck has vomited up from the recesses of your breast whatever wind it held. For they say: "If you follow only what is old, then the fasts of Moses and the miracles that Elisha worked when he raised a dead man are condemned by you." What reason has a competent examiner found here? Even if a pale searcher for gold came along, he would not find in your thoughts the run of hidden veins, nor would a miner of words let light into unaccustomed hiding-places. Do we, then, fail to approve venerable miracles because we do not consent to youthful excesses? If, mindful of the Gospel, we subject the servant to the master and the disciple to the teacher, do we neglect whatever could be of use? There are other things, most shameless of men, which we bring into recent use without injury to antiquity.

Next you have opened up a new charge, one which our inquiry had passed over: "Why did the pope convene a synod, without the precedent of an earlier example, to examine the charges of crimes against him?" After this you accuse us of falsehood, because we say that what was written in the aforesaid business was requested from the prince. Grant, Lord, that we may get past the winding turns of this labyrinth without straying; direct the path which the twisting serpent makes after the fashion of its own body or mind, so that we may truly say: The Lord of hosts is with us, our helper is the God of Jacob; and rejoice with Solomon, who says: The horse is prepared for the day of battle, but all protection is with the Lord. It is indeed superfluous to answer absurd propositions, since the prophet says: Do not answer a fool according to his folly. But if anything is passed over in contempt, I fear that it may be thought that fear kept us from touching it, as though it were strong. It is better for us, with blessed Paul, to cut off the grounds for insult and to testify with full voice: I have become foolish; you compelled me. Was it, then, without any example that the pope convened a council of bishops, he at whose discretion a synodal assembly is gathered? Or were the crimes of yours that might be condemned by this multitude trifling? Are the words of the canons not direct, that any cleric who departs from his bishop before the time of sentence on an uncertain suspicion remains under manifest censure? For the service of this matter a band devoted to God had to come together, so that an army of physicians might relieve the sores of a lost and ruined flock; for whenever the violence of diseases hastens with swift step to the inner places of the soul, saving counsel cannot bring helping hands except from the consultation of many. For our petition also asked this of the king, that, the prejudgements of the clergy being cut away, the heavenly power might judge through human mouth concerning the merit of the pope's accusers. Let us look, however, if you please, and read again those subtleties of your instructive pamphlet, having also before our eyes the sanctions of the fathers, by which the bilge of your excesses may be weighed. Church law requires that a pontiff accused by others is not to be deserted before the charges have been established in the light. But you, mindful, I suppose, of divine law, who despise light errors, who rejoice in the nobility of sin, so that no single fault from deserting your bishop might regard you, accused [him] with increments of offences. To this strength he who is your leader brought you, that after the pontiff had been abandoned and assailed, you believed that the censure of the bishops of almost all Italy, without the force of any sentence, was to be disapproved: as someone said of your band: He did not entrust the soul hastening to death to a single [death]. Can you, untaught mind, already enriched by the successes of crimes, rest from your detestable purpose as if exhausted? He made you rich in these evils whose abundance of pride took away his angelic wealth, and who, out of the treasure of harm in which he abounds, envied the divine endowment.

But, mindful of our promise, let us touch on all the things which we recall were inserted in their work. Pope Symmachus is accused, in a most splendid style, of having entered the examination with throngs of people, anticipating the summons, and of having afterwards scorned the judgements when he had been summoned four times. Has love of the truth so departed from you that you think the testimony of the world is wrapped in clouds of lies, and believe that words painted with the brush of deceit have more strength than the truth which Rome holds? Did he, then, either approach the hearing unseasonably or flee it when he was awaited? Did not expectation, rather than fury, call out that multitude of people devoted to God, out of Christian zeal for the faith? Does anyone who runs to inflict violence have tears for companions, and does one who is eager to cause fear show the face of one who fears? That multitude, joined to the bishop's ministry, brought us laments, not javelins; nor did it come menacing with weapons, but pitiable with weeping, to burden your purpose only by being seen, because with rich streams from its eyes it showed how lamentable your harshness had made the condition of the man assailed, and in the sobriety of the venerable examination it commended by its own affliction him whom it could not commend by voice. But from this you have it plain what fury kindles your bile: that he came to the judgements almost acquitted, for whom the world weeps; and while in your speech you gather against the aforesaid an odium foreign to the facts, your neck, long proud, is bowed for a little to reverence for us. For you call on the sacred assembly at the moment when you wish to declare Symmachus our destroyer, and with cruel piety you think that whatever he lost while sitting in the citadel of the churches accrues to our honour. Not only have we not felt these things, but we feel the opposite: turn the poisons of your protection rather upon others. He has not the testimony of a defender who pays the service of his mouth to one who resists it; he who grants something to one unwilling loses what he thinks is the gratitude for a benefit, because there is no gift except what you are willing to receive.

Now there is no need of long admonition for those already lost: we owe hatred to the work, of whose authors there remains nothing more to condemn. You assert that crowds of women, with city colours, came to the judgements with the aforesaid, and by that subtlety of yours the sex is displayed which should have had greater affection for its bishop. Most profane of men, I hold it written: It is one thing to speak ill, another to accuse; and that the prophet said: Rejecting the word, you have put your hope in calumny and in tumult, and you are in it; therefore this iniquity shall be to us as a breach; because God says on our behalf: But those who judge you, I will judge. And again he says to his servants: Do not fear the reproach of men, and do not be afraid of their blasphemies. Again also he cries out to you: Come here, seed of the adulterer and the fornicator: at whom have you jested, at whom have you opened wide your mouth and thrust out your tongue? Are you not wicked children, a lying seed?

Notice what you join to these, when you say: "With the case unheard, his defenders abandoned, the pope withdrew," setting before us in the present business examples from the forum and the streets, whose hypocrites you are. For us it is written by the apostle Paul: those to whom the world is crucified, what have they to do with the forum? But you do not know these things, or, what is graver, you despise what you know. I suppose the pope withdrew demanding something strange and divorced from reason. Did he not, constrained by pastoral care for the state of the tottering church, hope for what both religious foresight and the order of the case itself demanded? For what form of judgement had gone before, when, we having been torn apart in hostile fashion and the church's wealth carried off even at your instigation, he who had long been food for the hungry seemed to have been made a slave of hunger, while the distributor lacked nourishment, so that there was servitude in lordship and lordship in servitude? What precedent of a former age, handed down through memory, brought this into the open? What could a man convicted by a sentence be made, in whose case the judgement came before the hearing? There was no privilege of which one already stripped could be despoiled. You thought one help remained to you in the sacred assembly: to join bishops to yourselves as companions in defending the enormity of crimes, so that the deed might go unpunished through the pollution of many. A judge is never called in at a fitting time when he is summoned to a business almost decided: even if the guilty man has deserved [it], the accuser takes it away, who wishes more to be allowed to his own fury against him than to the judge. For the prophet, attacking you, says: This is the portion of those who laid us waste, and the lot of those who plundered us. Go, swift angels, to a flock torn and mangled, and to a terrible people. To you an angel has been sent, namely through the bishops, by whose voice and merit they receive the gifts to be borne to Christ, and, the Lord being appeased, grant to mortals the prayers obtained; through whom the rejected gifts of concord were offered to you; who brought the rewards of love to those deserving punishment; who, while they considered themselves, in nothing regarded what you deserved.

"Who saw him," they say, "engage in open battle, as they put it, with his accusers?" Most shameless of men, consider whom you wish to fight with whom, and, if any sense of salvation remains in you, attend to the places, times and persons of both sides; and if the wickedly heaped-up wealth of a still depraved heart has not subdued you, raise your eyes a little to God, and for even a short time despise the orders of your sinister counsellor. You recognise that you are not protected by the commands of the supreme king in those things which deservedly must be punished, because, although the terms of the request dictate the character of the reply, and the petition, coming first, describes what is to follow, yet you never caught the free words of the ruler in your nets, and imperial letters never served your desires through the snares of cunning. How often has the ineffective bite of harm snapped in empty gapings? How often has whatever you held in hope concerning the accused escaped you, and the image seized by presumption deserted you, empty-handed? Thanks be to God, who has put this foresight into him to whom he has committed the sum of human affairs. There is a sure hope of quiet and of safety in a ruler's perfect wisdom. The ship whose master is equipped with the gift of understanding for the governing of the helm has everywhere a mooring, everywhere a harbour among the waves. The security of all is certain when one trained in noble arts rules the state. The heaven-infused government of our emperor knows how to put up a hand against minds notorious for deceit. There is no need of labour before him whom naked truth long ago obtained as her defender. Let the impious cease to counterfeit simplicity with fraud before him: whatever moves itself against justice is soon caught; nothing is safer before the aforesaid than innocence; he who puts forward things agreeable to equity has a strong embassy; the flatteries of the unfaithful, which are often a grievous assault upon princes, are not read [by him]. But these things are better told to God, from whom the plant of this fruit descends.

The unwelcome condition of the work I have undertaken brings me back to you, I who until now wished to devote my effort to better discourse, while imperious necessity demands a captive speech. For you said: "How did you first deal with his case or its character, when the synod did not yet have firmness?" O brazenness of unclean speech and face of a pamphlet which ignorance has not alone stained! You both narrate and question the province of our deliberation. This is surely why we were in doubt: because, as you say, the synod did not have firmness; the nature of the business went beyond those who were to hear it, and more still remained in reverence for the man assailed than there was in the integrity of our college.

Next, in place of the torments of questioning, you repeat that the venerable bishops Laurentius and Peter suspended themselves from communion with the pope, and whatever the caution of those summoned provided for, you turn into a charge against the man attacked. Was there ever a time, then, while the sacred rites of the mass were being celebrated by them, when the commemoration of his name ceased? Did the bishops named ever, according to your wishes, offer half-complete sacrifices without the catholic rite and the ancient custom? Was offence ever given to God through grace, so that it might be ascribed to your head, and did the offering, the nurse of pardon, become the mother of sin? Those of whom you speak were indeed separated only by the meeting of the body; yet they did not avoid the presence of souls. If you think those are parted from mutual fellowship whom the clasp of religion joins, biting with a holy tooth, your feeling has led you far from the judging of faults. It is dwelling in the heavenly commandment that either unites us or separates us: it does not matter what distances keep us apart, if we are held in one chamber in the mansion above. Truly we infer from this that you are slaves of the belly and the body, and by this baseness of your opinion you declare yourselves to be earthly chattels. For it is written: The natural man does not perceive the things that are of the spirit.

After this, your ranks turned to flight, you added, in the manner of a frenzied speech: "Have, then, the councils of bishops decreed by the laws of the Church to be held yearly throughout the provinces lost their force because they do not have the presence of the pope?" Read, you utter madmen, whether anything was ever established in them apart from the sanction of the apostolic summit, and whether, if anything arose on the greater matters for conference, it was not reserved to the judgement of the aforesaid see. For so you have it: if any of the bishops has been deposed by a provincial judgement, let him appeal again, if he wishes, to the Roman pope, and let [the pope] himself, if it seems good, renew the judgement in aid of the condemned man. See, what you prepared as a snare is free of knots, unless perhaps we are bound in that part by the tightest bonds and the paths of reply do not lie open to us, while a track that was passable before is clothed with thorn bushes in a new blockage.

For with these brambles of speech you hold us back while we walk on level ground, when you say that the prince was injured because we wished at the very outset to have the visitor assigned [to us] withdraw, as being against the rules of the Church, so that nothing more might then be allowed to vices, lest the darnel harden, lest the profane harvest lie unfelled by any sickle of discipline before its ripeness, and it be thought permitted which the judges did not forbid. Hence it is openly clear that you are supported by the authority of no precedents apart from the excellence of the most pious king, whom you vainly long to link to the offence. It remains for me to show that he too is not bound up in these excesses, which befell [only] the good of all, because he wished the one sent to be not an occasion of litigation nor a fuel of quarrel, but a cause of concord, foreseeing, of course, that unless the protection of his commands fenced in a simple man, your poisons would soon steal him away as bait for dissension. For it is written: The simple man believes every word. Therefore he fixed a boundary to the mandate which it would not be allowed to violate by any transgression. He ordered the aforesaid, as soon as he had been brought to Rome, to go to meet [the pope] at the basilica of blessed Peter, making the king's command out of a bishop's wish. For who would not think the pontiff would willingly obey in that matter which the prince did not believe was permitted to himself, even if he were to forbid it? And there he ordered [him] to address the pope, once greeted by him, with his own mouth, so that he would hand over to his fellow bishop the slaves, to be subjected to no tortures, but kept, indeed, for the debate of the synodal examination. O purity of the command, which, while it carries a torch before present times, drives the ancient ones into shadow; which snatches the light from the old by the ill-omened splendour of novelty! What man rich in tongue, or what fabricator of reputation, ever attached this to anyone deservedly poor? Who has thus enriched with invented praises by report a lord beggarly in the truth of his deeds? I do not take from you the writers by whose kindness it has come about that the deeds of our ancestors have been brought down to us adorned; but I will not keep silent about the benefits of God, because our prince surpasses the ornaments of words by his deeds. He does not seek glory dependent on tongues: he believes that what is added to his praise is a lack of care. Look with what balance, as on a scale, the venerable weigher of cases examined [the matter], so that, although a skilful fulfilment was granted to your petition, he nevertheless guarded the laws of the Church in all things. What hearts, however much sharper than others, are sufficient for such judgement? At one time, by one writing, without loss to equity, your desires are fulfilled, and the same document is directed both to the service of religion and to your joy. For the inquiry of a good prince foresaw that the assertion of slaves was not to be proved by the examination of an innocent man. For in the choice of the venerable judges he himself repelled the accusers as out of order, he himself restored the accused to hope.

Let us see, however, if these things were done, whether you were not enemies of God and also of your earthly lord, while you despise Christ and the king with equal rashness, and one course of crimes has led you to both insults. The bishop who was sent is snatched away by the coils of your mouth from the very threshold of fulfilling the command, and he who had come to fight for peace is fitted to be an incitement to confusion. Without visiting the threshold of the blessed apostle, already not himself, he is summoned to the service of your fury, and that foundation of churches which draws the devout from all the hinges of the world, set close by, is passed over: [while] it is not permitted to approach a mediocre building. Then, separated from the root, he lost the hope of good fruits. You may perhaps say that the apostle's spirit is diminished if a citizen of heaven is thought to be enclosed in places on earth. Yet although blessing is granted everywhere to those who ask, and the faith and devotion of the suppliant demand the presence of the martyr, it cannot be denied that more is granted to care on the native soil, and that the places from which one passes to heaven obtain greater affection. The multitude of cures has already lent credit to this claim, and after diabolical possession we have witnesses already healed. Although these things are celebrated through our Redeemer in the whole world, still no small nobility has been acquired by that monument through the throng [of pilgrims], because through him who changed a man into an angel the nature of earth could be made illustrious. You begrudged your visitor this grace, reckoning that he would cease to be a follower of your errors if he had touched the inner sanctuary of the revered passion. See, you have no support in the royal authority; see, after the heavenly disturbance, the censure of the prince also, which you caused to be spurned, justly strikes you.

Let us see whether any defence remains from the proposition about the rules. "He himself," they say, "gave visitors to other bishops, and it is just that he be held by the law of his own act." I do not attack you on this head for falsehood; I do not refute words long clinging to lies; I say, however, that the maker of a law is not enclosed by the bounds of his own definition unless he wishes, and unless the prince governs the height of disdain, he is called in vain to the law he has given. There is a law of probity and of mind which chastises a man living without law: he who does not owe discipline to necessity pays it properly to his character. Perhaps God has willed to end the cases of other men through men: the bishop of this see he has reserved without question to his own judgement. He willed that the successors of the blessed apostle Peter owe their innocence to heaven alone and present an inviolate conscience to the search of the most subtle examiner. Do not think that those souls which God has reserved above others for his own examination have no fear of inquirers. Before him the guilty man has no help from the brilliance of pleading, since he has as witness of his deeds the same one he has as judge. You may say perhaps: such will be the condition of all souls in that trial. I will reply that it was said to one: You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven; and again, that by the voice of holy bishops the dignity of his see has been made venerable in the whole world, since whatever is faithful everywhere is subjected to it, since it is designated the head of the whole body, concerning which it seems to me it was said through the prophet: If this is humbled, to whose help will you flee, and where will you leave your glory?

What if, though I have unclean lips, washed by no waves of a kindled coal, as was granted to Isaiah, it were permitted to me to call forth the apostle Peter himself to defend the privileges of his possession, and he were to speak with human voice what he does by prayers? If you heard him, he would say this: "Sons of men, how long will you be heavy of heart? Why do you love vanity and seek a lie? Know that the Lord has made his holy one wonderful. Why do you long to undermine the foundations established by the hands of Christ? Why do you strike with a battering ram the ancient spirit of the possession of him who grows young through faults, and by the tearing apart of the Church's flock subject me to new sufferings even after the flesh? It is an unheard-of kind of sacrilege which you colour with the honour of a feigned religion: he dishonours the reverence of a venerable name who promises himself as a helper in the offences which he alleges committed against God. It is a kind of insult to stand by as if in support of one on high, according to the apostle: Who are you, to judge another's servant? Why do you mock unskilled ears and make the show of punishment heavier than that of guilt? If you owe hatred to excesses, cleanse yourselves. Why do you condemn crimes more freely than you avoid them? He is his own assailant who presses charges of adultery with the services of fornication and accuses [sins] of the flesh through the debauching of souls. Surely you remember it is written: Cursed are all who go whoring away from you. He, therefore, is loosed by a foul bond from the brightness of his Lord who pays his duties to the heavenly statutes with less than pure faith. The brightness of our possession, as I see, has stirred envy in you, which you transfer by feigned indignation at the evils of its possessor, while you sweat at the cost. The citadel by which you were made conspicuous, shaken by frequent blows, you would have undermined, had I not resisted, and shown by its ruin how great is the structure established by heaven. Do not look for victory from your own disaster: do not, by prevailing, lose the triumph won by my labours and my sweat. Whatever leads to a trophy, I have obtained: whatever would make you illustrious, I have gathered into the see. That torch gives you brightness which you think can be put out by viper's venom. He is kindled to his own destruction who so rages against the shoots of his own grace as to cut off the plants: anger freer than is just harms its author more than others."

"The things you call Symmachus' excesses, if they exist, I bear with the same expectation with which I bear you too: it is wrong for a sinner not to love the patience of the judge. What does he demand but vengeance, who, though guilty himself, finds fault with the delays of punishment in another? This word I owe to those zealous efforts, because I hold that God said that man is prone to wickedness and that all flesh is a friend to sins. I do not wish that, on account of one person, the possession that will give dignity to countless men should fall into abasement, lest, while a man is attacked, the divine law be broken. Believe me, if the things you say exist, I take note of them, because in those also of whom nothing of the kind was said, I have looked into what there was. He errs who believes that the one nearest to God can be deceived: Vengeance is mine, I will repay, says the Lord. Rather you, once sons, with whom spiritual childbirth burdened the womb, return to the concord you have forsworn: let mother church receive you into her loving bosom, as she has held you until now. Correction is never too late: she knows how to wait long for those sought with immense labour; she does not know how to despise as cheap those bought at a great price. The return to salvation is by many steps: no one is excluded except the one who despairs: let the fruit of pardon go next to the crown. Do not help pope Symmachus by your pressures: if he is guilty, believe me, when the ministry of human attack has ceased, divine judgement soon follows. Is not either punishment or reward due to the aforesaid [man] in the scale of the most splendid judge? Do not look to me for syllogisms and figures of speech. I still use the ancient net in pursuit of men, and I have not abandoned the skiff mocked by the wise of the world. It bears me up through the straits of the world: the net that you see, proved in the catching of men, enriches me."

"Return, then, since flight has not yet carried you off into wildness: run to the fold, lest you expose yourselves to the ambushes of wolves, lest through delay you lose the grace of those who come of their own accord, since Gehenna follows an invitation scorned. If I owed any sweetness as a father, if I fulfilled any strictness as a teacher assigned by God, take care that a sparse crown of Levites does not much longer surround whatever corner of my cross, lest a solitude grievous even to outsiders reign for long, lest the labour of my womb should, in place of sterility, have borne a hostile household, and a numerous offspring show by wicked deeds the barrenness of the one who bore it. Few are the things I have asserted, but reckon how much hangs on them. Come, sons, hear me: I have taught you the fear of the Lord. Look at Rome, which the shedding of Christ's blood made free from the slavery of idols without the price of gold or of silver, on which he ordered even my death, the death of his little servant, to be spent; which for many ages offered worship at famous shrines; which long venerated, in images of demons, the terror that a master's hand had set up at great cost of wealth; which looked up to the power of deities bought with the price of metals; for which the more practised hand of the craftsman produced loftier gods, and the divinity that man conferred by his workmanship had among men a greater form than God. See, now by Christ's favour the statues have gone back to new furnaces; see, now your use receives from an outworn superstition something to rejoice in, while from the old Thunderer new vessels are rightly made. Why do you strive to break this quiet? Why mock happiness with vain efforts? This madness has no excuse, believe me: it makes no difference by what roads he runs to the prince of the world who defects from holy unity: he who saddens the church offers fat victims to the devil. Reject, then, vain snares: the love of peace has a simple defence: he is fully armed who scorns the weapons the adversary supplies to discord: the bare opposition of faith suffices against all the darts of quarrels. Why, seeking consolation for evils, do you bring back into the open the times of Eulalius and Boniface? Why do you set old contagions before the growth of excesses, and by an unjust will allow antiquity no power to cover offences? There was then another cause of discord, and if I were not forced, in narrating, to endure things past, I would show you that no consolation comes from comparing the deeds, because those whom a zeal compliant with partisanship had raised to the pontifical summit, I rejected both, I chose this one, because of those, as the outcome witnesses, none pleased me; of these, I made a fugitive of the one striving against the rules, and preserved the one lawfully promoted while the world attacked him. You know these things, and they are not new, because, while that one was thrust out and this one confirmed, your assent fought for me."

"Next, why, to your own ruin, do you wound the council of bishops? Why do you tear at the sentence in which, by Christ's inspiration, heavenly oracles were revealed and the tongue of the pontiffs stood as interpreter between God and men? Why do you make the grief of the whole church out of [a wrong] committed in one [church], even if the chief one? For that court of heaven, enriched with the endowments of various curule seats and adorned with much gold and purple of our Redeemer, produced nothing in that decision on its own authority, but through the ministry of the human tongue served the divine command. It understood that whatever it decreed under [divine] impulse was not its own: it has nothing in that sentence except that for which it may rejoice in devotion alone: the pen felt a foreign eloquence, taking from it only this glory, that it both kept and honoured what was poured into it. Why have you prepared slander out of these gospel examples? As is written of you: They erred through drunkenness, they did not know the seer, they were ignorant of judgement. For while you strike with profane words the men named, you betray both ignorance and malice. Did these men, then, not believing the resurrection of the body which they preach, mix themselves with heretical contagions? Do these men pursue in their heart what they abjure with their tongues? So, because they said that he is to be feared who can kill the body and send the soul into Gehenna, did they therefore weave things foreign to the faith? See, profound ignorance! Look at blessed Luke, by whose assertion you can be refuted, who cries: Fear him who, after he has killed the body, has power to send the soul into Gehenna. What room for error is there here, where the words of the example and of the narrative concur in fitting agreement on an equal course, and what is put forward does not differ from the catholic understanding and the readings? A knot is never rightly sought in a bulrush: mists do not envelop those who preach the author of light. Do they, then, not believe in the resurrection of the flesh because they confess that the body can be killed, that a sinful soul can be delivered over to Gehenna? Your heart is choked with thick briars and strives to ascribe its inner vices to others. You also boast that the writings of the apostle John were violated, because it was said in his words: If we say that we have no sin, we are liars, and the truth is not in us. I make no complaint about the difference between manuscripts. Were the apostle's admonitions corrupted, then, because they did not add 'we deceive ourselves', and because they added 'we are liars' — you who are ignorant not only of divine but even of human reason? He who does not have the truth is rightly judged a liar, and he who is known to be empty of integrity is full of nothing but falsehood. But these things in us are not to be cured by the speech of the tongue but by that of groans, and words should no more be offered to you than tears, since he is clearly guilty who sets against the innocent either the desert or the name of a culpable man."

"The remaining heads of your objections I will not go over: it is better that things deserving condemnation be buried in silence. He gives renown to crimes who passes on their airing to the ears of posterity by repeated report. The opinion of blessed Paul is to be followed, who admonishes all through his disciple and cries: Avoid empty questions. For there are many things in your propositions which the love of sinning embraces with such filthy arms that they become unworthy of mention; more are disgraced by levity, while your words are disembowelled with their weight withdrawn and windy speech is composed on matters of religion, having won a gravity suited only to the ear, which in its abundance of chaff will bring nothing of wheat into the barns, while it brings forth an abundance of stalks barren of grain and from the luxuriance of the grass deceives the farmers' hope. Those things in which the winnowing fans find no profit are owed to the fire and will perish in burning: of these it is written: The men [of riches] slept their sleep, and found nothing. Nothing, dearest ones, is sweeter than peace, provided a breast full of bitterness does not shut out its savour. I owed you a briefer admonition, which no small regard for you, and a brow in you long exercised in quarrels, drew out at length. It is usual for many sinners not to be corrected by a terse address, and the effusiveness they had in their offences they require in the words of the one admonishing them. It is enough for me to have complied both with your care and with the heavenly commands. In what is to follow I will leave no room for words, because I report this: that Rome, the head of the world, has been laid low by your efforts, and that the chair, the nurse of the pontificate, sees itself despised like the lowest seat."

His voice blessed Paul took up and thundered with that freedom of speech which he always used, attacking the prince of the apostles for his leniency, because toward flighty and abandoned minds he still kept a parent's affection and did not succour with the healing iron ulcers driven deep, teaching that hidden diseases must be cut out with blades and that a salutary wound must be applied to manifest desperation, lest, while the doctor's hand is held back by impiety from cutting corrupt flesh, death be invited by refraining from the knife; because, while the right hand spares the sick, it kills those it should cure, and there is no great difference whether you inflict death or permit it. He who could shut out death from the sick and does not has inflicted it. With these words, then, he opened the door of his mouth against them:

"Whoever you are who judge, in that in which you judge another you condemn yourself: for you who judge do the same things. And we know that the judgement of God is according to truth against those who do such things; and again: Blessed is he who does not judge himself in what he approves. What evil reasoning is this, that one who steals should preach that one must not steal, and should clothe a brow prodigal of shame in the cloud of attacking another? No one rightly takes on the part of an admonisher unless he condemns errors by his own acts and shows a love of innocence in his way of life. For even tax-collectors can condemn in speech the vices dear to their own habits, and by the more wicked offices of the tongue punish what they love, as if it were not a kind of greater excess to give with the lips affection to a thing you despise in your mind, and to clothe the venom of your character in the honey of conversation. I act in this way as if you had shame, chastity, grace of feeling, or as if anyone were allowed to accuse a teacher and fit the bites of a livid mouth against one who is elect, when beforehand, foreknowing what was to come, I had warned you with full voice in the letter given to you: Who shall bring accusation against the elect of God? It is God who justifies: who is he that condemns? And again: O man, who judge those who do such things and do them yourself, do you think that you will escape the judgement of God? Or do you despise the riches of his goodness and patience and long-suffering? You accuse wickedness, being filled with iniquity, fornication, avarice, malice, envy, murders, condemnation, deceit, malignity, proud, arrogant, inventors of evils, disobedient to a parent, foolish, disorderly, without affection, without mercy. You teach that no one should mingle with fornicators, you who are either the followers or the forerunners of the adulterer Laurentius, through whom he either put forth the poisons he had or received those which he showed by pouring them out. After that stain of an enticing communion, a plague execrable to the whole world, you blame the bishops of God as if they were incorporated in a sullied communion: you think those guilty who entered into fellowship, though convicted by no witness, and you follow a man pierced through, I will not say by the pen, but by the sword of the whole ecclesiastical indictment. What is lawful is not lawful, and what is not lawful is lawful. Just as Jannes and Jambres withstood the truth, so you too are reprobate in mind, traitors concerning the faith, insolent, puffed up, lovers of pleasure more than of God, having indeed the appearance of piety but denying its power. O force of inner grief, which cannot set out what it has conceived, which bursts through the urge to speak that it commanded, thrust into the depths of the heart! I will say nothing more to you: what remains of my speech, laments will supply."

After this, if you grow sicker under the doctors' treatment and no regard for your salvation brings you back from what you have begun, at least look to your city, the parent of the world: she herself, after her defenders the apostles, approaches you mourning; she herself addresses you and, if any dutiful affection remains [in you], begins a speech that will win its plea:

"Behold me, made conspicuous, whom the temples of the most high God made to rejoice in the splendour of a new light, once the worship of the shrines was repudiated; me, whom, after filthy chapels polluted with much gore of cattle, the outpouring of the Lord's and the apostles' blood cleansed from the blood of victims; me, whom health, restored after long fevers, made despise the sanctuaries; me, whom the offering freed from victims; I who acquired the peace of Christ through enmity with idols; I, to whom gifts were hardly more numerous than gods; me, whom my religion made a beggar through its varied devotions; me, whom poverty had crushed as I constantly asked favours of my gods; I who sent to Tartarus the Curii, the Torquati, the Camilli, whom the church did not regenerate, and the rest, an unfruitful mother of a most numerous offspring, while I wasted away, ill delivered, with my womb exhausted; because the saving of their country did not redeem the Fabii, and the glory won with much sweat availed the Decii nothing. Innocence of works without faith was ruined: Scipio, most observant of justice, was joined to the criminal, because he did not know Christ. I would wish to draw my pen through the whole of my infancy, if the breast of a bereaved woman could bear it. But whoever rereads past things worthy of lamentation seems to desire times of tears. No one is believed to have grieved over those whose recounting does not wound him: he who keeps a dry face while recounting the deaths of his children is convicted of cruelty by a sure witness. That posterity, lost, brought more grief than, acquired, it brought joy. Let us review, nevertheless, by what successes these things have been changed. Behold, now in that sanctuary of liberty nothing servile is found from the worship of idols; behold, the crown of honours, the genius of the world, the Roman flower, tramples in full sanctity the altars it long venerated; behold, now my senate house is called to heaven, praised, received, and I cannot say that after the grace of baptism I have lost any offspring, even one that sudden death took away. The supreme Ruler embraces many holders of the trabea and the curule chair without loss of their dress or dignity; now the munificence of an earthly triumph almost purchases divine favour, and this profits for the grace of Christ, that you strive to be held venerable by the world. I lie, unless needy throngs await the coming of your consulship as a relief of their miseries; for your purple, with which you ennoble the name of the year, drives off by the largesse of clothing the cold that steals upon the wretched; now almost again the glories of the fasti bring help to necessities, and the old unbelief laid aside, by such provision the expenses of wealth are made gains for souls. Behold, now the wet thresholds of the apostolic confession send candidates to the portable chair, and with abundant tears, joy exacting them, the gifts conferred by God's kindness are doubled."

"At a time when we dry our breasts with precious offspring, when the eternal mother now receives our progeny to bear them again, whose womb after the first birth is filled with aged offspring, who by regenerating it makes sweet to me the progeny I bore, who makes those coming to her put off old age and the broken return to the beginnings of life — who, I ask, exchanges this happiness for disputation? Who, through discord sown by a viperish mind, orders the blessings of my golden age to perish? Who secretly breathes ruin into my renewal and, under the appearance of a smooth brow, gains strength for enmities? I do not recognise a noble lineage in such business. If, however, there are any of the highest rank whom the storm of this tempest has joined to the base, they are stained by sharing in crimes of which others are the authors. Splendour of blood, even if it incurs a share in crimes, does not know how to offer itself as leader to sinners. It may perhaps bear guilt for neglected caution; it does not deserve punishment for leadership in wickedness. He who is called into quarrels already grown is joined to wrongdoers with a certain shame: he in whom only easy credulity is censured does not deserve the despair due to the lost. It is rather you I see, sprouts of the crossroads, you I recognise, in whom the baseness of nature has produced habits suited to itself, for whom to have degenerated would have been distinction, who, under the title of a feigned religion, rejoice in the impunity of vices, whose lips the taste neither of honours nor of quiet has ever touched, who violate every right by obeying your origin, whom the present cause has shown, brought out of hiding places and caves. Who, before the contriving of this evil, knew who you were? Long you cherished the secret places in which the night of your birth had hidden you from us. Return rather to the blindness dear to you: leave to us the clear light of day: grant the church concord either by your absence or by your correction. If, however, you wish to be counted among splendid lineages, I will recognise it by the amendment of your deeds."
